tasks.title: The history of Halloween
tasks.instruction: Read and judge the statements.
tasks.passage: Halloween grew out of the ancient Celtic festival of Samhain, which marked the end of the harvest season and the beginning of winter. The Celts believed that on the night of October 31 the boundary between the living and the dead became blurred, so they lit huge bonfires and wore animal skins to confuse restless spirits. When Irish immigrants brought the tradition to America in the 19th century, cheap and plentiful pumpkins replaced turnips as lanterns. 'Trick-or-treating' developed later, partly from the medieval practice of 'guising', where people performed small tricks in exchange for food. Today Halloween is a multi-billion-dollar holiday, yet its central idea remains the same: one night a year when people enjoy being frightened.

statements.text: Samhain celebrated the start of the harvest.
The Celts thought spirits could walk the earth on that night.
Pumpkins were used as lanterns before turnips in Ireland.
Trick-or-treating has links to medieval customs.
Modern Halloween has lost its original idea completely.

tasks.title: The economics of fear
tasks.instruction: Read and judge.
tasks.passage: Psychologists distinguish 'recreational fear' — horror experiences sought out voluntarily — from trauma, which is imposed. Studies of haunted-house visitors show that excitable personalities report greater enjoyment, suggesting the pleasure comes less from the stimulus itself than from the sense of mastery: surviving the scare confirms our competence. Economists add another layer. Fear-inducing entertainment generates outsized revenue precisely because its physiological arousal — elevated heart rate, dopamine release — is shared socially; co-regulation turns individual alarm into group bonding. Critics counter that commercialised horror flattens the folkloric function of Halloween, which historically processed collective anxieties about death and the changing seasons through ritual rather than profit.

statements.text: Recreational fear is chosen freely by the experiencer.
Research links enjoyment purely to the intensity of the scare.
Shared physiological arousal can strengthen social bonds.
Critics argue commercial horror preserves folklore's function.

tasks.title: Style editor
tasks.instruction: Click the unnatural/incorrect word and fix it.
tasks.sentence: Hardly had we entered the cellar than we heard a scream.
tasks.explanation: 'Hardly ... when' (not 'than'). 'No sooner ... than' uses 'than'.

tasks.title: Inversion
tasks.instruction: Rewrite starting with the word in brackets.
tasks.source: We had barely entered the cellar when we heard a scream.
answers: hardly had we entered the cellar when we heard a scream
tasks.explanation: Hardly had + subject + past participle ... when + past simple.
